input.question: If one company buys out another company for a monetary fee, wouldn’t the money go back to the parent company, therefore the parent company essentially gained capital for free since they own the other company? How does that work?
input.ground_truth: No, because when the company is bought it is bought from its owners. You know, the shareholders? They get the money from the buyout. The only way it would stay with the company is if the company owned itself which is silly.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: If one company buys out another company for a monetary fee, wouldn’t the money go back to the parent company, therefore the parent company essentially gained capital for free since they own the other company? How does that work?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a lemonade stand (that’s your company), and your big brother has a huge toy store (that’s the bigger company). Now, your big brother really likes your lemonade stand, so he gives you some of his toy money to buy your lemonade stand from you.

Now, your lemonade stand belongs to your big brother. The money he gave you? That was his own money, so now he doesn’t have as much toy money as before. But now, he has your lemonade stand too! So, he didn’t get extra money—he just traded some of his toy money for your lemonade stand.

It’s not like he got money for free. He spent his own money to get something new (your lemonade stand), so now he has to take care of both the toy store and the lemonade stand. If the lemonade stand makes more money, that’s good for him, but he didn’t get free money—he just bought something new.

So, when a big company buys a smaller one, they use their own money to get the smaller company, and they don’t get extra money—they just get something new that they hope will help them make more money in the future.
